analysis.one_liner: Phases in a national zero-emission car sales mandate reaching 100% by 2035.
analysis.headline: S. 3845 was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on February 29, 2024 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require automakers to sell a rising share of zero-emission vehicles in the U.S. each year starting in model year 2027 — 43% that year, climbing to 100% by 2035. Companies that fall short would have to buy zero-emission vehicle credits from companies that exceed the targets, or pay a civil penalty of twice the value of the credits they failed to submit. After 2035, the EPA could order manufacturers to stop making any passenger vehicle that is not zero-emission.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially the tens of millions who live near highways and freight corridors, would benefit from less soot and smog, which the bill's findings say cause thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses each year. Drivers would eventually benefit from lower fuel and maintenance costs of electric vehicles, and communities facing climate-driven disasters would benefit from cutting transportation pollution, the largest U.S. source of greenhouse gases.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a binding schedule so that 43% of new passenger vehicles sold must be zero-emission by model year 2027, rising yearly to 100% by 2035.
Creates a tradeable credit market, letting manufacturers that sell more clean cars than required sell credits to those that fall short, and directs civil penalty payments into the Highway Trust Fund.
Preserves states' rights to set stricter zero-emission vehicle rules of their own, as California and other Section 177 states currently do.

The bill's findings cite eliminating soot and smog that cause thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses every year, and reducing pollution from transportation, the largest source of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers bear the compliance costs of converting their fleets to electric on a fixed schedule, and they would pass much of that cost to new-car buyers through higher prices. The oil industry loses a growing share of its largest market as gasoline demand shrinks. Households without reliable home charging or in rural areas could face the biggest squeeze, since they would be buying from a shrinking pool of gas models at rising prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is technology-specific: it requires battery or hydrogen vehicles rather than setting emissions limits and letting automakers choose how to comply, which raises the risk of higher new-vehicle prices on a fixed timeline regardless of whether charging networks, grid capacity, and battery supply chains are ready.

Rural households, apartment dwellers without home charging, and low-income buyers could be hit hardest if used-car and remaining gas-model prices rise before charging access catches up; the bill's own sense-of-Congress language urging manufacturers to "diversify vehicle technologies and models" acknowledges the consumer-choice concern.

A single national standard would override the incremental, state-by-state pace that states like California have set, forcing faster change in states that may not be ready; the credit-trading design also hands a valuable new revenue stream to early EV adopters like Tesla, a cost ultimately absorbed by the rest of the industry and its customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health and climate gains are large and well documented — vehicle exhaust is a leading source of the pollution that causes asthma, heart disease, and premature death. But the bill is an aggressive design choice: a hard sales mandate with fixed percentages, rather than a flexible emissions standard, concentrates the transition risk on automakers' balance sheets and, ultimately, on new-car prices. Whether it helps or hurts an individual household depends heavily on access to charging and timing of purchase. It is a high-stakes bet that infrastructure and supply chains can keep pace.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2024 on February 29, 2024, with Senator Whitehouse as the sole cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; no further action was taken.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee, so it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep selling gasoline vehicles on their existing timeline, and the oil industry keeps its vehicle-fuel market intact. Anyone counting on a faster national shift to clean cars gains nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 29, 2024 and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it attracted.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Carper (D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; both sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill also never advanced in the Democratic-chaired committee, so the partisan shape of a floor fight was never tested.

industries.note: The bill forces a full fleet conversion to zero-emission vehicles on a fixed schedule, with civil penalties for shortfalls — but it also creates a tradeable credit market that rewards companies that move early. Compliance costs would largely be passed to new-car buyers. The industry broadly favors a slower, more flexible transition, which is why a hard mandate died without even a hearing.

Companies already selling large volumes of zero-emission vehicles would earn credits they can bank, sell, or trade, turning their existing position into a revenue stream. Their interest in the mandate runs alongside the public's interest in more clean cars, though the credit value is ultimately paid by the rest of the auto market.

A 100% zero-emission sales requirement by 2035 steadily shrinks the market for gasoline, the industry's core retail product. Its interest in stopping the bill runs against the public-health case for eliminating vehicle exhaust.

Dealers are expressly excluded from the definition of vehicle manufacturer, so they face no direct compliance obligation, but a fast electrification shift would change their sales mix, service revenue (fewer gas-engine repairs), and inventory costs.
